title: Shloka 37
subtitle: Kula, and what lies outside it

namas.translation: She is the well-born woman of the lineage, the one whose presence makes the household a household.

compound.gloss: the woman belonging to the kula

children.gloss: family, noble lineage; the tantric assembly
a woman of well-rounded limbs, a woman

namas.translation: She has her seat inside the kula itself, not somewhere outside it looking on.
The left-hand path that takes the whole body and the whole world as material for worship belongs to her.

morphology.note: A taddhita derivative of kula rather than a compound: kaula with the feminine suffix, she who belongs to the Kaula observance.

namas.translation: Among the powers that make up the kula she is the yoginī, the one whose practice joins them into one.

compound.gloss: the yoginī who belongs to the kula

children.gloss: a woman practised in yoga, a goddess of power

namas.translation: Above the whole ordered assembly of powers is a place where the ordering stops, and she is there too.

morphology.note: A negative compound: read as a nañ-tatpuruṣa, she who is not the kula, though it can equally be taken as a bahuvrīhi, she for whom there is no kula.

compound.gloss: not the kula, beyond the assembly of powers

namas.translation: The inward discipline that dispenses with outward rite is where she is found.
Of the two ways of worshipping her she is herself given over to the inward one.

compound.gloss: wholly given to the observance of the samaya

children.gloss: the conduct prescribed by the samaya
conduct, customary practice, rule of behaviour

commentary.meaning: Seven names, the most crowded verse anywhere in this stretch, and six of them turn on a single word. She is the woman of the kula; she has her seat inside the kula; she is Kaulinī, she of the Kaula way; she is the yoginī of the kula. Then the fifth name takes the floor out: akulā, not the kula, outside the whole assembly. And the last two step across to the other term of the tradition's long argument with itself — she abides within the samaya, and she is wholly given to the samaya's way of doing things. In seven names the hymn has named both of the rival forms of its own practice, placed the goddess squarely inside each of them, and put between them a name saying that she is not inside anything. It is the most doctrinally loaded verse in the batch, and it takes no side at all.
commentary.history:
The Śrīvidyā tradition has argued for centuries about what kind of tradition it is, and this verse is the passage both parties quote.

On one side is the kaula stream, which worships the goddess in the external diagram with a full ritual apparatus, and which historically included practices — the five substances beginning with wine — that mainstream Brahminical opinion regarded as transgressive. On the other is the samaya stream, which holds that the real worship is internal, conducted in the centres of the body, and that the outward rite is at best a concession. The two are not different religions; they share the mantra, the diagram and this hymn. They disagree about what to do on a given evening.

The disagreement has a documented history in the commentaries. Lakṣmīdhara, whose commentary on the Saundaryalaharī is one of the best known, reads that poem throughout as a samaya text and is openly hostile to kaula practice. Bhāskararāya, writing in the eighteenth century and the most influential commentator this stotra has ever had, was himself a kaula and read accordingly. Both of them had this verse in front of them. Bhāskararāya could point to four consecutive names built on kula and to Kaulinī standing in the middle of the line; a samayin can point out that the verse gives the last word to samayācāratatparā, wholly devoted to the samaya observance, and that the goddess is described as tatparā, given over to it, in a way she is not said to be given over to anything kaula. The hymn will not settle it. It was probably not written to.

The word kula is doing several things at once across these names and it is worth separating them. Kulāṅganā is the plainest: aṅganā is simply a woman, and kulāṅganā in ordinary non-technical Sanskrit means a respectable married woman of a good family — the mistress of a household. The tradition has taken an entirely conventional social term and made it a name of God, and the effect is the same as the effect of calling her mother in the very first name of the hymn. Kulāntasthā and kulayoginī use kula in the technical sense of the assembly of powers: she is not observing the kula from outside, she has her station in it, and among its members she is the one whose practice binds them together. Kaulinī is a derivative rather than a compound: kaula with the feminine ending, she who belongs to the Kaula observance.

Akulā is the pivot. Read as a simple negation it says that she is not the kula, that she stands outside the assembly of powers altogether. But akula has a second life. Monier-Williams, working from ordinary classical usage and with no interest whatever in tantra, records akula as a name of Śiva. In the Kashmirian traditions that is the standard technical usage: akula is Śiva, the ground, the unmoving, and kula is Śakti, the unfolding. On that reading akulā is not a denial of anything but a claim of identity — the feminine form of the masculine ground, she who is Śiva. The hymn has placed the word at the exact centre of the verse, between four kula names and two samaya names, which is either a very good accident or a very deliberate piece of construction.

Samaya has a range as wide as kula's, and it overlaps with the saṃketa of the previous verse almost exactly: agreement, compact, convention, established observance, precept. So the two verses have used two different words for the same idea, once as the kula's private compact and once as the samayin's rule of conduct, which suggests that whoever assembled these names was aware of writing a bridge. There is also a piece of external evidence worth having. In the Saundaryalaharī, Samayā appears twice not as a doctrine but as a proper name of the goddess herself, standing beside a masculine partner — in verse 39 as the great Samayā beside the god who presides over the fire of the svādhiṣṭhāna, and in verse 41 as the one who dances the gentle lāsya while her partner dances the tāṇḍava. So samayāntasthā may be saying something more concrete than devotion to a school of practice: she abides within Samayā, that is, within her own name.
commentary.practice:
Seven names in thirty-two syllables makes this the most broken-up verse in the batch, and the groupings are uneven: four, four, three and five in the first line, then three, five and eight in the second. Nothing else in this stretch of the hymn has that shape. Count it out once — kulāṅganā, kulāntasthā, kaulinī, kulayoginī; akulā, samayāntasthā, samayācāratatparā — and then chant it, and the irregularity becomes the character of the verse rather than an obstacle.

The most useful warning in this whole batch belongs here. Akulā has a short initial a. Lengthen it and you have said ākulā, which is a real Sanskrit word meaning confused, agitated, flurried, overburdened. One misjudged vowel turns beyond the assembly of powers into in a flap. Say a-ku-lā crisply, with the first syllable as light as you can make it.

The verse is built on a drumbeat. Ku-la at the head of four consecutive names, then a-ku-lā, which is the same two syllables with a single short one bolted on the front to reverse the sense. Then sa-ma-ya twice. If you let the alliteration carry, the doctrinal shape of the verse becomes audible without any explanation: four beats of one thing, one beat of its negation, two beats of the other thing.

Three clusters need care. Kulāṅganā has ṅg, the guttural nasal at the point of the g. Kulāntasthā and samayāntasthā both have the sequence n-t-s-th across a syllable boundary, which is four consonants with no vowel among them: say kulān-tasthā, releasing the t before the s begins and putting the aspiration on the th alone. And kaulinī opens with the diphthong au, which is long and must not be shortened toward o — this is the vṛddhi vowel again, here as the marker of a derivative: kula gives kaula the way sundara gives saundarya.

Samayācāratatparā is the only long name in the verse and it has one seam: samaya plus ācāra, two a-sounds fused into a long ā. Four short a's, then a long ā, then tatparā with two more shorts. The rhythm of that word alone is the reason the second line does not feel top-heavy.

One point on the dental n. Every nasal in this verse except the ṅ of kulāṅganā is a plain dental — aṅganā, kulānta, kaulinī, yoginī, samayānta. Not one retroflex ṇ in thirty-two syllables, which after four verses thick with them is worth hearing as a deliberate change of colour.

This verse and the last are the two favourites for archanā, the form of recitation in which each name is turned into the dative and offered with a flower or a grain of rice. Seven short names in one verse means seven offerings in the time the previous verses would have taken for two. It is worth practising this one both ways — kulāṅganā becoming kulāṅganāyai namaḥ, kaulinī becoming kaulinyai namaḥ — since the ā-stem and ī-stem datives behave differently and this verse gives you four of one and three of the other.

On what to hold: the verse describes two ways of doing this and says that she is in both of them, and then says she is in neither. If your own practice tends strongly one way — toward ritual and its objects, or toward the inward work with nothing in the hands — this is the verse that declines to congratulate you.

crossReferences.translation: In your root-support centre, together with Samayā who is given to the gentle dance, I contemplate the nine-fold one, dancer of the great tāṇḍava in its nine flavours. Out of the compassion of that pair, intent on bringing things into being, this world of ours was born and had them for its father and mother.
crossReferences.relevance: Samayā used as a proper name of the goddess rather than as the name of a school, and paired with a male dancer in the lowest centre of the body — the same centre the stotra reaches in the next verse but one. Read against samayāntasthā it suggests that the name may be saying she dwells within Samayā, that is, within herself, and not merely that she approves of a particular style of worship.

crossReferences.source: A verse on the Kaulas, widely quoted from the Kulārṇava Tantra and elsewhere
crossReferences.translation: Śāktas within, Śaivas without, and taken for Vaiṣṇavas in company: wearing one form and another, the Kaulas move about on the earth.
crossReferences.relevance: The self-description of the party whose name stands in the middle of this verse. Given in translation only, because the Sanskrit circulates in several different wordings and none of them could be checked against a printed edition. What it describes is not hypocrisy but a rule of concealment, and it is the practical face of the guardianship of the compact that the previous verse attributed to the goddess herself.

references.title: The Secret of the Three Cities: An Introduction to Hindu Śākta Tantrism
references.author: Douglas Renfrew Brooks (University of Chicago Press, 1990)
references.note: The clearest account in English of the kaula and samaya positions, what actually separates them in practice, and how a single lineage in south India managed to hold both. Read it before deciding what this verse is saying.

references.title: The Saundaryalaharī, or Flood of Beauty
references.author: W. Norman Brown (Harvard Oriental Series 43, 1958)
references.note: Brown's introduction discusses Lakṣmīdhara's samaya reading of the Saundaryalaharī and its polemical edge. It is the best short demonstration that these two words name a real dispute between real people and not a scheme invented by scholars.

references.title: The Doctrine of Vibration

references.note: For akula. Dyczkowski works through the Kashmirian use of kula and akula for Śakti and Śiva at length, which is the background that makes the fifth name of this verse something other than a flat negation.

references.note: Look up akula and then ākula, one after the other. The first is glossed among other things as a name of Śiva; the second means confused and agitated. They are separated by a single vowel length, and this verse contains one of them.
